title: Simplax: Enriching Discrete Diffusion Without Changing Its Noise
hook: Discrete diffusion is boxed in by its corruption kernel. Simplax bolts a continuous simplex variable onto each noisy token — richer training signal, same underlying categorical process.
key_points: In discrete diffusion the corruption kernel fixes both the intermediate state space and the reverse prediction problem, which limits how the objective can be built.
Simplax augments each corrupted categorical state with an auxiliary simplex-valued (Dirichlet) variable, chosen so the original uniform diffusion is preserved exactly as the categorical marginal.
The augmentation buys a tractable Rao-Blackwellized reverse-bridge objective plus a matching stochastic reverse sampler — a lower-variance training signal, not a different noise process.
The denoiser still takes only the corrupted categorical state as input, so the extra variable costs nothing at inference.
On unconditional OpenWebText generation it improves the generative perplexity-versus-entropy tradeoff, the standard way to check a sampler isn't buying fluency with collapsed diversity.
Trained only on 30-clue Sudoku, it was the most accurate of the compared methods at every clue density tested, including the hardest uniquely-solvable 17-clue case.
content_html: Discrete diffusion models generate categorical data — tokens, grid cells — by corrupting them and learning to reverse the corruption. The corruption kernel is doing a lot of quiet work: it decides what the intermediate states look like and, with that, what the reverse prediction problem even is. A team spanning Japanese and Singaporean institutions asked whether you can enrich the training objective and the reverse transitions without touching that kernel at all. Their answer, posted to arXiv in August 2026, is Simplax.
extra_html:
The trick is an exact Dirichlet-categorical augmentation: pair every corrupted categorical state with a continuous variable living on the probability simplex, arranged so that marginalizing the new variable out recovers the original uniform diffusion exactly. Nothing about the noise process changes; what changes is that the richer joint admits a Rao-Blackwellized reverse-bridge objective and a matching stochastic reverse sampler. Rao-Blackwellization is the classic move of conditioning on extra structure to cut estimator variance — here it means a cleaner training signal for the same underlying problem. The denoiser's input stays the plain categorical state, so inference is unchanged.

The authors report a better generative perplexity-versus-entropy tradeoff on unconditional OpenWebText generation, and on Sudoku a model trained only on 30-clue puzzles led the compared methods at every clue density they tested, including the 17-clue minimum for a uniquely solvable puzzle, along with the highest validity in unconditional generation. See the paper for the derivation and the full comparison set.

related.title: What Does a Discrete Diffusion Model Learn?
related.hook: A discrete diffusion model can be read as a denoiser, a score, or a bridge predictor. This paper proves they're the same optimum in different coordinates — with one exact best solution.

flashcards.prompt: What does Simplax add to uniform discrete diffusion, and what does it deliberately leave alone?
flashcards.back_html: It couples each corrupted categorical state with an auxiliary simplex-valued variable. The categorical corruption process itself is untouched — the original uniform diffusion is preserved exactly as the marginal of the augmented process.

flashcards.prompt: Why does Simplax's auxiliary simplex variable not make the model more expensive to sample from?

choices.text: The denoiser still takes only the corrupted categorical state as input
The auxiliary variable is discarded after the first reverse step
The simplex variable is computed once and shared across all timesteps
Sampling falls back to the unaugmented model at inference time

flashcards.explanation_html: The augmentation reshapes the training objective and reverse bridge, but the network's input signature is unchanged, so the extra variable never has to be produced at inference.

flashcards.prompt: What made the Sudoku result notable?

choices.text: A model trained only on 30-clue puzzles stayed most accurate down to the 17-clue minimum
It solved every puzzle it was shown during training without error
It was the first diffusion model applied to constraint-satisfaction problems
It needed no clues at all to generate valid grids

flashcards.explanation_html: Training at a single clue density and still leading at every density tested — including the hardest uniquely-solvable regime — is evidence the improvement is in the learned reverse process, not in matching the training distribution.
